traces.name: evidex_query_C01
traces.query: We are a mid-sized lender that has only ever reserved for loan losses once they looked probable. Under the US lifetime expected-loss standard, what actually changes for us - in the timing of provisions, the information we must use, our equity and regulatory capital, and the data we need to keep - and why did standard-setters decide the old approach was inadequate?
traces.answer:
Under CECL (ASC 326), you would record an allowance for all expected lifetime credit losses on assets carried at amortized cost from origination or purchase, with no probable threshold. The allowance is measured using past events, current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts. The day-one allowance and later changes run through earnings, and the transition hit goes to opening retained earnings. Standard-setters judged the incurred-loss model too late in recognizing losses. The excerpts do not quantify the effect on your institution, and they do not establish which regulatory capital category you fall into.
- **No recognition trigger.** Current GAAP delayed recognition until a loss was probable. The new standard removes that threshold and reflects management's current estimate of all expected credit losses [ASU_2016-13 p9; OCC ACL Handbook p6].
- **Day-one charge.** An allowance is recorded at origination or purchase, and a credit loss expense is recognized in net income in most cases [Implementation Handbook p20]. For non-PCD assets, recording the initial allowance produces a credit loss expense; for PCD assets it does not [Implementation Handbook p203].

Layer management adjustments only for risks the modelled estimate does not already capture. traces.query: For a large credit-card book, how should the expected-loss allowance be built - which balances need a reserve and which do not, how should cardholders be grouped, and how do repayment assumptions drive the size of the reserve - and what would examiners specifically test?
traces.answer:
The excerpts cover the general CECL framework and some credit-card-specific points. They do not contain a credit-card reserve formula, worked numbers, or the full "Credit Card Portfolios" examination section, so the answer below is limited to what they state.
- **Funded balances are in scope.** Credit-card balances carried at amortized cost are measured under CECL. The bank estimates expected losses over the remaining lives of the funded card loans [FDIC FAQ p12; Implementation Handbook p127].
- **Unfunded available credit generally does not need a reserve when it is unconditionally cancellable.** Where the bank can cancel available credit at any time, it records no allowance for unfunded commitments, even if it has a past practice of extending credit before detecting default. Only the funded balance is measured [ASU_2016-13 p144 (Example 10, 326-20-55-54 to 55-56); Implementation Handbook p127; FDIC FAQ p12]. Examiners will therefore need to confirm that the cardholder agreements actually permit unconditional cancellation.
